title: Ephemeral residency resonance during windowed continuous batching - allocator debugging
creator: Leah Kim
description: Intermittent growth in resident GPU pages observed under our windowed continuous-batching workload. Unlike steady-state slab bloat we've seen before, this shows rhythmic "residency resonance" where resident pages increase in pulses correlated to prefetch windows and long-lived streams. Goal: identify allocator behavior root cause, reproduce reliably, and land a low-risk mitigation for the 1.21 release.
reproduction_steps: Run synthetic continuous-batching harness (tools/loadgen/windowed_kv_prefetch.py) with window_size=64, prefetch_depth=8, mix=kv-heavy, concurrency=24
Observe baseline for 10m, then enable 'aggressive-prefetch' flag (runtime config) to mirror customer workload A
Capture GPU memory snapshots every 30s via nvml (nvmlDeviceGetMemoryInfo) and cudaMemGetInfo in-app logging
Collect per-stream allocation traces with the kernel debug allocator build (runtime build: debug-alloc/2026-02-28) and run for 30 minutes
Record system metrics (CPU, host staging bytes, swap activity) and runtime metrics (pool residency, deferred_free_queue_length) to Grafana dashboard 'runtime/mem/kv-prefetch-res'
observations: Resident GPU memory increases in ~90–120s pulses of ~180–260MB before partially releasing; net growth across a run is positive (plateau only after ~40–50 minutes)
Deferred free queue length correlates with pulses; queue length spikes immediately after large prefetch batches finish
Pinned host staging buffer (host_staging_bytes) shows a monotonic increase, suggesting staging-to-device transfers are not fully coalescing frees
NVidia tools (nsight) show many small device allocations from the same arena with noncontiguous residency — indicating internal fragmentation
Runs without prefetch or with prefetch_depth<=2 do not exhibit pulses, pointing to prefetch window as a trigger
investigation: Collected malloc/free traces using env RUNTIME_ALLOC_LOG=1 and matched with stream IDs; observed that frees are issued on separate non-default streams after kernel dispatches
Inspected cudaMallocAsync pool attributes via cuMemPoolGetAttribute equivalents and saw pool.hard_limit unset; default heuristics allowed large arena growth
Reproduced behavior on Ampere and Hopper hardware; magnitude varies but pattern remains — less pronounced on GPUs with larger page sizes
Run with CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES single GPU and added clocked dumps: the pattern persists, ruling out multi-GPU migration issues
Tested trimming heuristics: calling cudaMemPoolTrimTo to force coalescing reduces peak but causes short spikes in latency for a few requests
experiments: Experiment A: disabled cudaMallocAsync (fallback to cudaMalloc) — eliminated pulses but increased per-request latency by ~12% and increased CPU-side overhead
Experiment B: lowered prefetch_depth to 2 — eliminated pulses with minimal QoR changes for synthetic workload
Experiment C: forced stream-synchronization before pool trim — reduced net growth but introduced a 50–150ms tail latency regression in high-concurrency paths
Experiment D: set device mempool attribute 'release_threshold' to a conservative value (via cuMemPoolSetAttribute) — reduced fragmentation and peak residency by ~30% at moderate loads
Experiment E: implemented quick coalescing freelist (local branch) — promising in loadgen but needs safety review and broader perf tests
root_cause_hypothesis: Under windowed continuous batching with aggressive KV prefetch, many small device allocations are created across multiple non-default streams and then freed asynchronously. cudaMallocAsync's pool heuristics allow arena growth and delayed coalescing, producing rhythmic pulses of resident pages (ephemeral-residency resonance). Additionally, host staging allocations (pinned pages) are being retained due to stream-ordered deferred frees, preventing the system from releasing backing pages promptly.
mitigations_tried: Lower prefetch_depth configurable at runtime (works but reduces throughput headroom)
Explicit stream synchronization in staging path before trimming (reduces residency but harms tail latency)
Adjust mempool trim thresholds (bakery-config) to favor earlier trimming — reduces steady-state but risks more cuda calls
Fallback to cudaMalloc for very small allocations (<256B) to avoid pool fragmentation — mitigates pulses but increases CPU time
proposed_fix: Short-term (release-1.21): Add adaptive prefetch limiter that reduces depth under high deferred_free_queue_length; expose as runtime flag and default-on for Dedicated customers

Medium-term: implement epoch-based deferred-free draining: allocate an epoch token per request window; when epoch advances, issue coalesced trims on a low-priority background stream (avoids syncs on hot paths)
Long-term: update allocator to group small allocations by lifetime class and prefer per-lifetime mempools (reduces cross-stream fragmentation) and upstream recommended cudaMemPoolSetAttribute tuning
Add an internal OSS-style regression test (loadgen scenario) that asserts resident memory growth < 50MB over 30m under windowed prefetch workload
risks_and_tradeoffs: Epoch-based draining reduces tail impact versus immediate syncs but adds complexity and potential for delayed reclamation if epochs misalign
Grouping by lifetime reduces fragmentation but increases internal allocator state and may increase code-path complexity for cross-request sharing
Aggressive trimming increases CUDA API traffic and can raise per-request latency on spikes
Fallbacks to cudaMalloc remove pool benefits for small allocations and will raise per-token cost
next_steps: (Maya) Land adaptive prefetch limiter behind feature flag and run canary on staging cluster (canary: runtime-1.21-canary-memfix)
(Leah) Add resident-memory synthetic regression to CI load test harness and create Grafana alert 'mem.residency.delta>50MB/30m for kv-prefetch'
(Rafael) Prototype epoch-based deferred-free draining as an opt-in branch for performance validation
Schedule a 1-hour cross-team review with infra and perf on 2026-03-15 to validate release trade-offs
